claim: Malaria is caused by parasites of the genus Plasmodium.
source: Malaria is caused by parasites of the genus Plasmodium.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the causative agent of malaria.

claim: Of at least six Plasmodium species that infect humans, Plasmodium falciparum is responsible for the vast majority of the approximately 600,000 annual malaria-associated deaths.
source: Of at least six Plasmodium species that infect humans, Plasmodium falciparum is responsible for the vast majority of the approximately 600,000 annual malaria-associated deaths (World Health Organization, 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the World Health Organization 2022 report.

claim: The particular severity of P. falciparum malaria is largely due to the cytoadhesion of the infected red blood cell (iRBC) to the endothelium of the host vascular system.
source: The particular severity of P. falciparum malaria is largely due to the cytoadhesion of the infected red blood cell (iRBC) to the endothelium of the host vascular system.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the mechanism of P. falciparum pathogenesis.

claim: Cytoadhesion is mediated by the Plasmodium falciparum Erythrocyte Membrane Protein 1 (PfEMP1), a surface protein family of ~60 variants.
source: Cytoadhesion is mediated by the Plasmodium falciparum Erythrocyte Membrane Protein 1 (PfEMP1), a surface protein family of ~60 variants, which bind to different endothelial receptors including ICAM1, CD36, EPCR, and Chondroitin Sulfate-A (CSA) (Baruch et al., 1996; Salanti et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Baruch et al., 1996 and Salanti et al., 2004.

claim: PfEMP1 variants bind to different endothelial receptors including ICAM1, CD36, EPCR, and Chondroitin Sulfate-A (CSA).
source: Cytoadhesion is mediated by the Plasmodium falciparum Erythrocyte Membrane Protein 1 (PfEMP1), a surface protein family of ~60 variants, which bind to different endothelial receptors including ICAM1, CD36, EPCR, and Chondroitin Sulfate-A (CSA) (Baruch et al., 1996; Salanti et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Baruch et al., 1996 and Salanti et al., 2004.

claim: Cytoadhesion-induced accumulation of iRBCs in the vasculature of various organs, particularly the brain and placenta, can lead to fatal outcomes for the patient.
source: Cytoadhesion-induced accumulation of iRBCs in the vasculature of various organs, particularly the brain and placenta, can lead to fatal outcomes for the patient.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the pathological consequences of cytoadhesion.

claim: PfEMP1 is trafficked through the parasite's secretory pathway into the parasitophorous vacuole, then exported by the PTEX translocon into the RBC.
source: PfEMP1 is trafficked through the parasite's secretory pathway into the parasitophorous vacuole, then exported by the PTEX translocon into the RBC.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about PfEMP1 trafficking.

claim: PfEMP1 is believed to be transported via protein complexes called J-dots into Maurer's clefts.
source: Here it is believed to be transported via protein complexes called J-dots into Maurer's clefts (Külzer et al., 2012; Behl et al., 2019; Kriek et al., 2003), which are membranous sorting stations established by the parasite (Przyborski et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Külzer et al., 2012; Behl et al., 2019; and Kriek et al., 2003.

claim: Maurer's clefts are membranous sorting stations established by the parasite.
source: Here it is believed to be transported via protein complexes called J-dots into Maurer's clefts (Külzer et al., 2012; Behl et al., 2019; Kriek et al., 2003), which are membranous sorting stations established by the parasite (Przyborski et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Przyborski et al., 2003.

claim: Around 20 hr post-infection (hpi), PfEMP1 is translocated onto the RBC surface and assembled into parasite-derived knob protrusions.
source: Around 20 hr post-infection (hpi), PfEMP1 is translocated onto the RBC surface and assembled into parasite-derived knob protrusions (Crabb et al., 1997; Watermeyer et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Crabb et al., 1997 and Watermeyer et al., 2016.

claim: The process of PfEMP1 surface translocation is poorly understood.
source: This process is poorly understood, and it is unclear whether other surface proteins, such as the immunomodulatory RIFIN family proteins, are trafficked by the same machinery (Goel et al., 2015; Saito et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an inference based on the current state of scientific knowledge.

claim: It is unclear whether other surface proteins, such as the immunomodulatory RIFIN family proteins, are trafficked by the same machinery as PfEMP1.
source: This process is poorly understood, and it is unclear whether other surface proteins, such as the immunomodulatory RIFIN family proteins, are trafficked by the same machinery (Goel et al., 2015; Saito et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Goel et al., 2015 and Saito et al., 2017.

claim: Coinciding with PfEMP1 surface translocation is an increase in RBC rigidity, likely through re-arrangement of the RBC spectrin cytoskeleton.
source: Coinciding with PfEMP1 surface translocation is an increase in RBC rigidity, likely through re-arrangement of the RBC spectrin cytoskeleton (Rug et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Rug et al., 2014.

claim: Parasite proteins which are exported into the host cell mediate the assembly of knobs on the iRBC cytoskeleton and the trafficking of PfEMP1 via Maurer's clefts.
source: Parasite proteins which are exported into the host cell mediate the assembly of knobs on the iRBC cytoskeleton and the trafficking of PfEMP1 via Maurer's clefts.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about exported parasite proteins.

claim: Knob-associated histidine-rich protein (KAHRP) is a key component of the knobs.
source: Knob-associated histidine-rich protein (KAHRP) is a key component of the knobs (Rug et al., 2006), and a subset of proteins from the Plasmodium helical interspersed subtelomeric (PHIST) family interact with the PfEMP1 cytosolic domain and are thought to anchor it to the erythrocyte cytoskeleton (Oberli et al., 2014; Yang et al., 2020; Proellocks et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Rug et al., 2006.

claim: A subset of proteins from the Plasmodium helical interspersed subtelomeric (PHIST) family interact with the PfEMP1 cytosolic domain and are thought to anchor it to the erythrocyte cytoskeleton.
source: Knob-associated histidine-rich protein (KAHRP) is a key component of the knobs (Rug et al., 2006), and a subset of proteins from the Plasmodium helical interspersed subtelomeric (PHIST) family interact with the PfEMP1 cytosolic domain and are thought to anchor it to the erythrocyte cytoskeleton (Oberli et al., 2014; Yang et al., 2020; Proellocks et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Oberli et al., 2014; Yang et al., 2020; and Proellocks et al., 2014.

claim: Seven proteins have been specifically designated as PfEMP1-trafficking proteins (PTPs) due to the loss or reduction in surface PfEMP1 presentation upon their deletion.
source: Seven proteins have been specifically designated as PfEMP1-trafficking proteins (PTPs) due to the loss or reduction in surface PfEMP1 presentation upon their deletion (Maier et al., 2008; Carmo et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Maier et al., 2008 and Carmo et al., 2022.

claim: FIKK4.1 is important for efficient surface translocation of the PfEMP1 variant Var2CSA and its adhesion to its receptor CSA.
source: We have previously shown that a parasite-exported kinase belonging to the FIKK family, FIKK4.1, is important for efficient surface translocation of the PfEMP1 variant Var2CSA and its adhesion to its receptor CSA, as well as for modulating iRBC rigidity (Davies et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Davies et al., 2020.

claim: FIKK4.1 is important for modulating iRBC rigidity.
source: We have previously shown that a parasite-exported kinase belonging to the FIKK family, FIKK4.1, is important for efficient surface translocation of the PfEMP1 variant Var2CSA and its adhesion to its receptor CSA, as well as for modulating iRBC rigidity (Davies et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Davies et al., 2020.

claim: Using a DiCre-mediated conditional FIKK4.1 knock-out and quantitative phosphoproteome analysis, 66 parasite and RBC proteins were identified that are phosphorylated in an FIKK4.1-dependent manner.
source: Using a DiCre-mediated conditional FIKK4.1 knock-out (Jones et al., 2016; Collins et al., 2013) and quantitative phosphoproteome analysis, we identified 66 parasite and RBC proteins that are phosphorylated in an FIKK4.1-dependent manner.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Jones et al., 2016 and Collins et al., 2013, and refers to previous experimental data.

claim: KAHRP, several PTPs, and PHIST proteins are among the likely substrates of FIKK4.1.
source: KAHRP, several PTPs, and PHIST proteins are among these likely substrates of FIKK4.1, as well as proteins involved in nutrient acquisition (Ito et al., 2017) and several proteins of unknown function.
evidence: This is an inference based on phosphoproteome analysis data.

claim: Proteins involved in nutrient acquisition are among the likely substrates of FIKK4.1.
source: KAHRP, several PTPs, and PHIST proteins are among these likely substrates of FIKK4.1, as well as proteins involved in nutrient acquisition (Ito et al., 2017) and several proteins of unknown function.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ito et al., 2017.

claim: Phosphorylation likely alters the dynamics of several FIKK4.1 substrates to ultimately influence PfEMP1 presentation.
source: Phosphorylation likely alters the dynamics of several of these proteins to ultimately influence PfEMP1 presentation, while other substrates may be non-functional or play a role in an unrelated phenotype.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the mechanism of FIKK4.1 action.

claim: Mutation of individual phosphorylation sites is rarely informative for understanding complex kinase-substrate interactions.
source: This is true for kinase–substrate relationships in general (Ochoa et al., 2020), and therefore mutation of individual phosphorylation sites is rarely informative for understanding the complex interactions at play.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ochoa et al., 2020.

claim: TurboID is a biotin-ligase that, if fused to a bait, biotinylates lysines on proteins within an ~10 nm radius.
source: TurboID is a biotin-ligase that, if fused to a bait, biotinylates lysines on proteins within an ~10 nm radius (Branon et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Branon et al., 2018.

claim: A protocol designed for enrichment and detection of biotinylated peptides rather than whole proteins allows identification of protein domains accessible to biotinylation.
source: By using a protocol designed for enrichment and detection of biotinylated peptides rather than whole proteins (Udeshi et al., 2017; Kim et al., 2018), we identify protein domains accessible to biotinylation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Udeshi et al., 2017 and Kim et al., 2018.

claim: FIKK4.1 conditional KO lines harboring TurboID fusions of KAHRP and PTP4 were generated to monitor protein dynamics in their vicinity in the presence and absence of FIKK4.1.
source: We generated FIKK4.1 conditional KO lines harboring TurboID fusions of two FIKK4.1 substrates, KAHRP and PTP4, allowing us to monitor protein dynamics in both these proteins' vicinity in the presence and absence of FIKK4.1.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental approach used in the study.

claim: Among the 17 exported FIKK kinases, modulation of PfEMP1 surface translocation is unique to FIKK4.1.
source: We show that among the 17 exported FIKK kinases, modulation of PfEMP1 surface translocation is unique to FIKK4.1, and that other surface proteins such as RIFINs are not affected by FIKK4.1 deletion, indicating a specific pathway for the surface translocation of this key virulence determinant.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Other surface proteins such as RIFINs are not affected by FIKK4.1 deletion.
source: We show that among the 17 exported FIKK kinases, modulation of PfEMP1 surface translocation is unique to FIKK4.1, and that other surface proteins such as RIFINs are not affected by FIKK4.1 deletion, indicating a specific pathway for the surface translocation of this key virulence determinant.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: There is a specific pathway for the surface translocation of PfEMP1.
source: We show that among the 17 exported FIKK kinases, modulation of PfEMP1 surface translocation is unique to FIKK4.1, and that other surface proteins such as RIFINs are not affected by FIKK4.1 deletion, indicating a specific pathway for the surface translocation of this key virulence determinant.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that FIKK4.1 specifically affects PfEMP1 but not RIFINs.

claim: A C-terminally tagged TurboID fusion of FIKK4.1 was generated using CRISPR/Cas9.
source: To do so, we generated a C-terminally tagged TurboID fusion of FIKK4.1 using CRIPSR/Cas9 (Birnbaum et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental method used, supported by a citation to Birnbaum et al., 2017.

claim: Clones were selected and PCR validated.
source: Clones were selected, PCR validated (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), and the specific labeling of proteins in the presence of biotin was validated by western blot (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Substantial biotinylation could be observed in FIKK4.1-TurboID transgenic parasites but not in NF54 wildtype controls.
source: Substantial biotinylation could be observed in FIKK4.1-TurboID transgenic parasites (hereafter called FIKK4.1T) but not in NF54 wildtype controls, where only minimal background biotinylation is present.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: In biotin-free media, some background labeling was observed within the parasite.
source: In biotin-free media, some background labeling was observed within the parasite, while the addition of biotin leads to substantial biotinylation of proteins within the parasitophorous vacuole and the red blood cell compartment, particularly at the iRBC periphery where FIKK4.1 is localized (Davies et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The addition of biotin leads to substantial biotinylation of proteins within the parasitophorous vacuole and the red blood cell compartment, particularly at the iRBC periphery where FIKK4.1 is localized.
source: In biotin-free media, some background labeling was observed within the parasite, while the addition of biotin leads to substantial biotinylation of proteins within the parasitophorous vacuole and the red blood cell compartment, particularly at the iRBC periphery where FIKK4.1 is localized (Davies et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1B and a citation to Davies et al., 2020.

claim: The PfEMP1 variant Var2CSA was trafficked normally onto the iRBC surface in the FIKK4.1-TurboID fusion line in the absence of biotin and after a 4 hr biotin pulse.
source: The PfEMP1 variant Var2CSA was trafficked normally onto the iRBC surface in the absence of biotin and after a 4 hr biotin pulse (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The FIKK4.1-TurboID fusion is expressed, active, and does not compromise FIKK4.1 function.
source: Collectively these data show that the FIKK4.1T fusion is expressed, active, and does not compromise FIKK4.1 function.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented in Figure 1.

claim: 101 parasite proteins and 39 human proteins showed at least a 1.5-log2 fold enrichment in the FIKK4.1T samples compared to NF54 at either timepoint.
source: In total, we quantified 101 parasite proteins and 39 human proteins that showed at least a 1.5-log2 fold enrichment in the FIKK4.1T samples compared to NF54 at either timepoint (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data.

claim: 62.3% of the 101 identified parasite proteins are predicted to be exported.
source: 62.3% of the 101 identified parasite proteins are predicted to be exported, a significant enrichment compared to the Plasmodium proteome which only contains ~8% exported proteins (Aurrecoechea et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data and a citation to Aurrecoechea et al., 2009.

claim: The Plasmodium proteome contains ~8% exported proteins.
source: 62.3% of the 101 identified parasite proteins are predicted to be exported, a significant enrichment compared to the Plasmodium proteome which only contains ~8% exported proteins (Aurrecoechea et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Aurrecoechea et al., 2009.

claim: The parasite proteins with the strongest enrichment include FIKK4.1 itself and three PfEMP1 trafficking proteins (PTP4, PTP2, and PTP3).
source: The parasite proteins with the strongest enrichment include FIKK4.1 itself and three PfEMP1 trafficking proteins (PTP4, PTP2, and PTP3), which are also predicted FIKK4.1 substrates (Davies et al., 2020; Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 1E and a citation to Davies et al., 2020.

claim: PTP4, PTP2, and PTP3 are predicted FIKK4.1 substrates.
source: The parasite proteins with the strongest enrichment include FIKK4.1 itself and three PfEMP1 trafficking proteins (PTP4, PTP2, and PTP3), which are also predicted FIKK4.1 substrates (Davies et al., 2020; Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Davies et al., 2020.

claim: The most abundant human proteins include members of the 4.1R complex.
source: The most abundant human proteins include members of the 4.1R complex, suggesting that FIKK4.1 specifically interacts with this complex (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: FIKK4.1 specifically interacts with the 4.1R complex.
source: The most abundant human proteins include members of the 4.1R complex, suggesting that FIKK4.1 specifically interacts with this complex (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is an inference based on the abundance of 4.1R complex members in the TurboID data.

claim: Substantial labeling of alpha-synuclein was found in the FIKK4.1 TurboID dataset.
source: Notably, we found substantial labeling of alpha-synuclein, which is mainly associated with vesicle trafficking in neurons (Lashuel et al., 2013), with no known role in RBCs.
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data.

claim: Alpha-synuclein is mainly associated with vesicle trafficking in neurons.
source: Notably, we found substantial labeling of alpha-synuclein, which is mainly associated with vesicle trafficking in neurons (Lashuel et al., 2013), with no known role in RBCs.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lashuel et al., 2013.

claim: Alpha-synuclein has no known role in RBCs.
source: Notably, we found substantial labeling of alpha-synuclein, which is mainly associated with vesicle trafficking in neurons (Lashuel et al., 2013), with no known role in RBCs.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge.

claim: There is a clear enrichment of exported Plasmodium proteins associating with FIKK4.1 at later stages (20% early versus 66% late).
source: There is a clear enrichment of exported Plasmodium proteins associating with FIKK4.1 at later stages (20% early versus 66% late) (Figure 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: FIKK4.1 is expressed and exported to the RBC periphery in early ring stages before most other exported proteins are present.
source: This is likely because FIKK4.1 is expressed and exported to the RBC periphery in early ring stages before most other exported proteins are present (Davies et al., 2020), increasing the relative proportion of human proteins at the early stage.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Davies et al., 2020.

claim: PTEX150 was ~37-fold more biotinylated at the 16 hr timepoint compared to the 40 hr timepoint.
source: This protein was ~37-fold more biotinylated at the 16 hr timepoint compared to the 40 hr timepoint.
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data.

claim: In later stages, the majority of FIKK4.1 protein is located within the RBC, rather than within the trafficking pathway.
source: In later stages it is likely that the majority of FIKK4.1 protein is located within the RBC, rather than within the trafficking pathway, and proteins biotinylated at this point are more likely to operate within the same subcellular niche.
evidence: This is an inference based on the temporal dynamics of FIKK4.1 localization.

claim: PTP4 and KAHRP were selected as sensors of the local protein environment upon FIKK4.1 deletion.
source: Of the 101 proteins identified in the proximity of FIKK4.1, we selected two candidates to use as sensors of the local protein environment upon FIKK4.1 deletion: PfEMP1-trafficking protein 4 (PTP4) and KAHRP.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: KAHRP is a component of the knob structures.
source: KAHRP is a component of the knob structures, whereas PTP4 was previously observed in punctate structures in the RBC cytosol (Rug et al., 2006; Jonsdottir et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Rug et al., 2006.

claim: PTP4 was previously observed in punctate structures in the RBC cytosol.
source: KAHRP is a component of the knob structures, whereas PTP4 was previously observed in punctate structures in the RBC cytosol (Rug et al., 2006; Jonsdottir et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Rug et al., 2006 and Jonsdottir et al., 2021.

claim: Both PTP4 and KAHRP have been identified as likely direct targets of FIKK4.1.
source: Both PTP4 and KAHRP have been identified as likely direct targets of FIKK4.1 (Davies et al., 2020) and are found in the TurboID dataset at approximately equal amounts at both timepoints, indicating an early interaction with the kinase.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Davies et al., 2020.

claim: PTP4 and KAHRP are found in the TurboID dataset at approximately equal amounts at both timepoints, indicating an early interaction with the kinase.
source: Both PTP4 and KAHRP have been identified as likely direct targets of FIKK4.1 (Davies et al., 2020) and are found in the TurboID dataset at approximately equal amounts at both timepoints, indicating an early interaction with the kinase.
evidence: This is an inference based on the TurboID data.

claim: Both PTP4 and KAHRP are important for the correct presentation of PfEMP1 in knobs on the erythrocyte surface.
source: Both proteins are important for the correct presentation of PfEMP1 in knobs on the erythrocyte surface (Maier et al., 2008; Horrocks et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Maier et al., 2008 and Horrocks et al., 2005.

claim: A TurboID cassette was integrated at the C-terminus of PTP4 or KAHRP in the FIKK4.1 conditional KO line using CRISPR/Cas9 and selection-linked integration.
source: A TurboID cassette was integrated at the C-terminus of PTP4 or KAHRP in this FIKK4.1 conditional KO line using CRISPR/Cas9 and selection-linked integration (Figure 2A; Birnbaum et al., 2017; Lee et al., 2019; Knuepfer et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental method, supported by citations.

claim: No difference in PfEMP1 surface translocation was observed between the transgenic parasite lines and FIKK4.1 cKO parental parasites or after a 4 hr biotin pulse.
source: No difference in PfEMP1 surface translocation was observed between the transgenic parasite lines and FIKK4.1 cKO parental parasites or after a 4 hr biotin pulse (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 2), indicating that PfEMP1 transport is not affected by the TurboID tag.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: PfEMP1 transport is not affected by the TurboID tag.
source: No difference in PfEMP1 surface translocation was observed between the transgenic parasite lines and FIKK4.1 cKO parental parasites or after a 4 hr biotin pulse (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 2), indicating that PfEMP1 transport is not affected by the TurboID tag.
evidence: This is an inference based on the flow cytometry data.

claim: The KAHRP-TurboID fusion had a different and substantially stronger banding pattern than PTP4-TurboID on western blots.
source: Western blots of biotin-treated parasites showed that the KAHRP-TurboID fusion had a different and substantially stronger banding pattern than PTP4-TurboID (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: RAP treatment did not result in obvious changes to the western blot banding pattern beyond potential differences in loading.
source: RAP treatment did not result in obvious changes beyond potential differences in loading, indicating that no prominent proteins in the vicinity of KAHRP and PTP4 are completely lost upon FIKK4.1 deletion.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: No prominent proteins in the vicinity of KAHRP and PTP4 are completely lost upon FIKK4.1 deletion.
source: RAP treatment did not result in obvious changes beyond potential differences in loading, indicating that no prominent proteins in the vicinity of KAHRP and PTP4 are completely lost upon FIKK4.1 deletion.
evidence: This is an inference based on the western blot data.

claim: KAHRP and FIKK4.1 show partial co-localization at the erythrocyte periphery, although FIKK4.1 appears to be positioned more toward the lumen of the cell.
source: Visualization of KAHRP and FIKK4.1 using structured illumination microscopy (SIM) revealed a partial co-localization at the erythrocyte periphery, although FIKK4.1 appears to be positioned more toward the lumen of the cell (Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: PTP4 localizes mainly at the iRBC periphery, with some puncta within the iRBC cytosol.
source: PTP4 also appeared to localize mainly at the iRBC periphery, with some puncta within the iRBC cytosol.
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: PTP4 co-localized only marginally with FIKK4.1 and was generally closer to the lumen of the red blood cell.
source: PTP4 co-localized only marginally with FIKK4.1 and was generally closer to the lumen of the red blood cell (Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: Treatment with biotin resulted in streptavidin-fluorophore labeling predominantly around the periphery of the erythrocyte for both fusion lines.
source: Treatment with biotin resulted in streptavidin-fluorophore labeling predominantly around the periphery of the erythrocyte for both fusion lines (Figure 2F and G and Figure 2—figure supplement 4), with puncta visible when focusing on the top of the cell (Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2F, G, and supplementary figures.

claim: Both PTP4 and KAHRP TurboID fusions were able to biotinylate FIKK4.1, resulting in its pulldown by neutravidin-coated beads.
source: Despite little overlap by IFA, western blot analysis shows that both PTP4 and KAHRP TurboID fusions were able to biotinylate FIKK4.1, resulting in its pulldown by neutravidin-coated beads, suggesting transient co-localization (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: The biotinylation of FIKK4.1 by PTP4 and KAHRP TurboID fusions suggests transient co-localization.
source: Despite little overlap by IFA, western blot analysis shows that both PTP4 and KAHRP TurboID fusions were able to biotinylate FIKK4.1, resulting in its pulldown by neutravidin-coated beads, suggesting transient co-localization (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is an inference based on the western blot data.

claim: In total, 3560 peptides were obtained across the PerTurboID datasets, of which 2272 were biotinylated.
source: In total, we obtained 3560 peptides across the datasets, of which 2272 were biotinylated (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data.

claim: All non-biotinylated peptides were excluded from the dataset, eliminating the background signal often observed using the classical BioID/TurboID protocol.
source: All non-biotinylated peptides were excluded from the dataset, eliminating the background signal often observed using the classical BioID/TurboID protocol.
evidence: This is a description of the data analysis approach.

claim: In the KAHRP-T dataset, 195 proteins were identified, while 150 were found in the PTP4-T dataset.
source: In the KAHRP-T dataset, we identified 195 proteins, while 150 were found in the PTP4-T dataset.
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data.

claim: All three proteins (FIKK4.1, PTP4, and KAHRP) are observed in each other's datasets, suggesting that they co-localize at least transiently.
source: All three proteins are observed in each other's datasets, suggesting that they co-localize at least transiently.
evidence: This is an inference based on the mass spectrometry data.

claim: PTEX150 was the only protein not predicted to be exported which appeared in all three datasets.
source: The export translocon component, PTEX150, was the only protein not predicted to be exported which appeared in all three datasets, highlighting the specificity of the TurboID labeling for proteins in the proximity of the three exported bait proteins.
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data.

claim: The identification of PTEX150 in all three datasets highlights the specificity of the TurboID labeling for proteins in the proximity of the three exported bait proteins.
source: The export translocon component, PTEX150, was the only protein not predicted to be exported which appeared in all three datasets, highlighting the specificity of the TurboID labeling for proteins in the proximity of the three exported bait proteins.
evidence: This is an inference based on the mass spectrometry data.

claim: Most biotinylation sites on the RHOPH complex are localized in the disordered domains not resolved by electron microscopy.
source: Most biotinylation sites on the RHOPH complex are localized in the disordered domains not resolved by electron microscopy (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Disordered domains are more likely to be surface exposed.
source: This is expected as disordered domains are more likely to be surface exposed.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about protein structure.

claim: Biotinylation sites 1321 and 1323 within Clag3.1 are partially buried within the RHOPH complex.
source: Interestingly, however, biotinylation sites 1321 and 1323 within the component Clag3.1 are partially buried within the complex, suggesting that a state exists where these sites are more exposed to the TurboID-fusion proteins, potentially upon insertion into the iRBC membrane.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: A state exists where biotinylation sites 1321 and 1323 of Clag3.1 are more exposed to the TurboID-fusion proteins, potentially upon insertion into the iRBC membrane.
source: Interestingly, however, biotinylation sites 1321 and 1323 within the component Clag3.1 are partially buried within the complex, suggesting that a state exists where these sites are more exposed to the TurboID-fusion proteins, potentially upon insertion into the iRBC membrane.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the structural data.

claim: RHOPH3 is biotinylated on both sides of its transmembrane domain.
source: RHOPH3 is biotinylated on both sides of its transmembrane domain, indicating that it was likely biotinylated in the soluble state represented by the structure, where the transmembrane domain is sequestered within the core of the complex during trafficking and both biotinylated sites are exposed to the cytosol (Schureck et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural analysis and a citation to Schureck et al., 2021.

claim: RHOPH3 was likely biotinylated in the soluble state where the transmembrane domain is sequestered within the core of the complex during trafficking and both biotinylated sites are exposed to the cytosol.
source: RHOPH3 is biotinylated on both sides of its transmembrane domain, indicating that it was likely biotinylated in the soluble state represented by the structure, where the transmembrane domain is sequestered within the core of the complex during trafficking and both biotinylated sites are exposed to the cytosol (Schureck et al., 2021).
evidence: This is an inference based on the biotinylation pattern and structural data.

claim: Twenty-nine PHIST proteins were identified in the PerTurboID dataset.
source: Twenty-nine PHIST proteins were identified in our dataset (Supplementary file 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data.

claim: PHIST proteins contain an alpha-helical PRESAN domain.
source: These proteins contain an alpha-helical PRESAN domain, a subset of which have been shown to interact with the cytosolic domain of PfEMP1 (Oberli et al., 2014; Yang et al., 2020; Proellocks et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citations.

claim: A subset of PHIST proteins have been shown to interact with the cytosolic domain of PfEMP1.
source: These proteins contain an alpha-helical PRESAN domain, a subset of which have been shown to interact with the cytosolic domain of PfEMP1 (Oberli et al., 2014; Yang et al., 2020; Proellocks et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Oberli et al., 2014; Yang et al., 2020; and Proellocks et al., 2014.

claim: There is a substantial reduction in biotinylation within the PRESAN domain itself as opposed to most of the surrounding sequences, despite no reduction in the number of lysines in this domain.
source: Mapping the location of either KAHRP- or PTP4-T-mediated biotinylation on these proteins demonstrates a substantial reduction in biotinylation within the PRESAN domain itself as opposed to most of the surrounding sequences, despite no reduction in the number of lysines in this domain (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Lysines in the PRESAN domain are likely occluded from biotinylation by protein–protein interactions, potentially with PfEMP1.
source: It is therefore likely that lysines in this domain are occluded from biotinylation by protein–protein interactions, potentially with PfEMP1.
evidence: This is an inference based on the biotinylation pattern.

claim: Neither KAHRP nor PTP4 contain transmembrane domains.
source: As neither KAHRP nor PTP4 contain transmembrane domains, their TurboID tags likely remain within the RBC cytosol and can only biotinylate protein domains in this compartment or within the trafficking pathway.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the structure of these proteins.

claim: The TurboID tags of KAHRP and PTP4 likely remain within the RBC cytosol and can only biotinylate protein domains in this compartment or within the trafficking pathway.
source: As neither KAHRP nor PTP4 contain transmembrane domains, their TurboID tags likely remain within the RBC cytosol and can only biotinylate protein domains in this compartment or within the trafficking pathway.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of transmembrane domains.

claim: Biotinylation is observed only at the N-terminus of Maurer's cleft protein SEMP1, suggesting its single transmembrane domain is inserted into the membrane with the N-terminus exposed to the RBC cytosol.
source: For example, we observe biotinylation only at the N-terminus of Maurer's cleft protein SEMP1, meaning that it is likely that its single transmembrane domain is inserted into the membrane with the N-terminus exposed to the RBC cytosol.
evidence: This is an inference based on the biotinylation pattern.

claim: Several Maurer's cleft proteins with N-terminal transmembrane domains appear to be inserted into the Maurer's clefts in the opposite orientation to SEMP1, with the C-terminus exposed to the TurboID tags.
source: Conversely, several other Maurer's cleft proteins with N-terminal transmembrane domains appear to be inserted into the Maurer's clefts in the opposite orientation, with the C-terminus exposed to the TurboID tags (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is an inference based on the biotinylation pattern shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Var2CSA is biotinylated only on the cytosolic C-terminal ATS domain.
source: The biotinylation of the surface proteins Var2CSA and RIFIN shows contrasting patterns, with Var2CSA biotinylated only on the cytosolic C-terminal ATS domain, while RIFIN is biotinylated on the N-terminal extracellular domain (Bachmann et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data.

claim: RIFIN is biotinylated on the N-terminal extracellular domain.
source: The biotinylation of the surface proteins Var2CSA and RIFIN shows contrasting patterns, with Var2CSA biotinylated only on the cytosolic C-terminal ATS domain, while RIFIN is biotinylated on the N-terminal extracellular domain (Bachmann et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data and a citation to Bachmann et al., 2015.

claim: RIFIN biotinylation likely occurs during the trafficking process where the N-terminal domain may be at some point accessible to the RBC cytosol, or within the parasitophorous vacuole.
source: It is likely that this RIFIN biotinylation occurs during the trafficking process where this domain may be at some point accessible to the RBC cytosol, or within the parasitophorous vacuole.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the biotinylation pattern.

claim: 35 proteins were identified for which almost all peptides are more biotinylated either by KAHRP or PTP4-TurboID fusions, likely reflecting their positions in the cell relative to the two proteins.
source: In Figure 3D, we have highlighted 35 proteins for which almost all peptides are more biotinylated either by KAHRP or PTP4-turboID fusions, likely reflecting their positions in the cell relative to the two proteins (Supplementary file 8).
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Among the 16 proteins more biotinylated by KAHRP-TurboID are several proteins known to localize to the erythrocyte periphery such as Clag3.1, LYMP, MESA, GARP, and PHISTb proteins.
source: Among the 16 proteins more biotinylated by KAHRP-TurboID are several proteins known to localize to the erythrocyte periphery such as Clag3.1, LYMP, MESA, GARP, and PHISTb proteins (Oberli et al., 2014; Proellocks et al., 2014; Ito et al., 2017; Davies et al., 2016; Tarr et al., 2014; Coppel et al., 1988), as well as human alpha-synuclein.
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data and citations to multiple studies.

claim: Proteins more closely associated with PTP4 include parasite chaperones HSP70x, PF3D7_0113700 (HSP40), and PF3D7_0501100 (HSP40), as well as host chaperone CCT8.
source: Proteins more closely associated with PTP4 include parasite chaperones HSP70x, PF3D7_0113700 (HSP40), and PF3D7_0501100 (HSP40), as well as host chaperone CCT8.
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data.

claim: The association of chaperones with PTP4 agrees with previous immunoprecipitation experiments suggesting that PTP4 interacts with J-dots which are enriched in chaperones.
source: This agrees with previous immunoprecipitation experiments suggesting that PTP4 interacts with J-dots which are enriched in chaperones (Külzer et al., 2012; Behl et al., 2019; Jonsdottir et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Külzer et al., 2012; Behl et al., 2019; and Jonsdottir et al., 2021.

claim: Var2CSA PfEMP1 is more biotinylated by PTP4 than KAHRP-T, despite the fact that KAHRP is thought to directly associate with the PfEMP1 intracellular domain.
source: Surprisingly, we found that Var2CSA PfEMP1 is more biotinylated by PTP4 than KAHRP-T, despite the fact that KAHRP is thought to directly associate with the PfEMP1 intracellular domain (Ganguly et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data and a citation to Ganguly et al., 2015.

claim: In both KAHRP and PTP4-TurboID RAP-treated parasite lines there was a loss of biotinylation in the kinase domain region of FIKK4.1 upon RAP treatment.
source: Since the kinase domain of FIKK4.1 is deleted upon RAP treatment, we found that in both KAHRP and PTP4-TurboID RAP-treated parasite lines there was a loss of biotinylation in this region, as expected (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: An increase in biotinylation upstream of the kinase domain was observed upon FIKK4.1 deletion, likely as the remaining N-terminus of the protein is more exposed to biotinylation due to loss of the folded kinase domain.
source: An increase in biotinylation upstream of the kinase domain was observed, likely as the remaining N-terminus of the protein is more exposed to biotinylation due to loss of the folded kinase domain.
evidence: This is an inference based on the biotinylation pattern shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The PerTurboID protocol can reproducibly detect changes in protein accessibility in both PTP4 and KAHRP-T lines.
source: This serves as a useful control for FIKK4.1 excision and illustrates the capability of the PerTurboID protocol to reproducibly detect changes in protein accessibility in both PTP4 and KAHRP-T lines.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: KAHRP and PTP4 display changes to protein accessibility on a local level upon FIKK4.1 deletion.
source: While KAHRP and PTP4 display changes to protein accessibility on a local level, other proteins show substantial changes to all biotinylated peptides.
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: PTP4 shows an increase in biotinylation in the C-terminus upon FIKK4.1 deletion, while the N-terminus appears mostly unchanged.
source: An increase in biotinylation upon FIKK4.1 deletion is observed in the PTP4 C-terminus, while the N-terminus appears mostly unchanged.
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: For KAHRP, the most substantial changes in biotinylation upon FIKK4.1 deletion occur around position 351–364.
source: For KAHRP, the most substantial changes occur around position 351–364 (denoted by asterisks in Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Position 351–364 of KAHRP encompasses predicted FIKK4.1 phosphorylation sites observed in previous phosphoproteomics experiments.
source: This section encompasses predicted FIKK4.1 phosphorylation sites observed in our previous phosphoproteomics experiments (Davies et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Davies et al., 2020.

claim: Both phosphorylated and non-phosphorylated versions of the biotinylated peptides encompassing position 351–364 of KAHRP are detected in the PerTurboID datasets.
source: In the PerTurboID datasets, both phosphorylated and non-phosphorylated versions of the biotinylated peptides encompassing this section of KAHRP are detected.
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data.

claim: The phosphorylated peptides of KAHRP become less abundant upon FIKK4.1 deletion due to the loss of kinase activity.
source: As expected, the phosphorylated peptides become less abundant upon FIKK4.1 deletion due to the loss of kinase activity.
evidence: This is an expected result based on the loss of kinase activity.

claim: Loss of phosphorylated peptides upon FIKK4.1 deletion leads to an increase in the relative abundance of the non-phosphorylated counterparts of the same sequence.
source: This leads to an increase in the relative abundance of the non-phosphorylated counterparts of the same sequence (see Figure 4B for schematic).
evidence: This is explained by the schematic in Figure 4B.

claim: ACS7 shows a similar effect to KAHRP around position 876, with loss of phosphorylated peptides upon FIKK4.1 deletion.
source: A similar effect is seen for the FIKK4.1 substrate acyl CoA synthetase 7 (ACS7) around position 876, whereas the nutrient channel component RHOPH3 is more phosphorylated at position 853 upon FIKK4.1 deletion, shifting the ratio of phosphorylated to non-phosphorylated peptides in the opposite direction (see Supplementary file 9 for non-phosphorylated/phosphorylated peptide ratios).
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data.

claim: RHOPH3 is more phosphorylated at position 853 upon FIKK4.1 deletion.
source: A similar effect is seen for the FIKK4.1 substrate acyl CoA synthetase 7 (ACS7) around position 876, whereas the nutrient channel component RHOPH3 is more phosphorylated at position 853 upon FIKK4.1 deletion, shifting the ratio of phosphorylated to non-phosphorylated peptides in the opposite direction (see Supplementary file 9 for non-phosphorylated/phosphorylated peptide ratios).
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data.

claim: The observations of phosphorylation changes in ACS7 and RHOPH3 are supported by earlier phosphoproteomics experiments.
source: These observations are supported by our earlier phosphoproteomics experiments (Davies et al., 2020) and demonstrate the ability of PerTurboID to detect changes in post-translational modifications without specifically enriching for modified peptides.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Davies et al., 2020.

claim: PerTurboID can detect changes in post-translational modifications without specifically enriching for modified peptides.
source: These observations are supported by our earlier phosphoproteomics experiments (Davies et al., 2020) and demonstrate the ability of PerTurboID to detect changes in post-translational modifications without specifically enriching for modified peptides.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: PTP3, SEMP1, and PF3D7_0702500 each show an increase in biotinylation upon deletion of FIKK4.1 at almost all sites in both datasets.
source: Most notably, PTP3, SEMP1, and PF3D7_0702500 each show an increase in biotinylation upon deletion of FIKK4.1 at almost all sites in both datasets, suggesting a more substantial change to the localization or the accessibility of the proteins (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 4C and D.

claim: The increase in biotinylation of PTP3, SEMP1, and PF3D7_0702500 upon FIKK4.1 deletion suggests a more substantial change to the localization or the accessibility of the proteins.
source: Most notably, PTP3, SEMP1, and PF3D7_0702500 each show an increase in biotinylation upon deletion of FIKK4.1 at almost all sites in both datasets, suggesting a more substantial change to the localization or the accessibility of the proteins (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: This is an inference based on the biotinylation pattern.

claim: SEMP1 and PF3D7_0702500 co-localize at the Maurer's clefts.
source: SEMP1 and PF3D7_0702500 co-localize at the Maurer's clefts (Dietz et al., 2014), while PTP3 appears to localize to the iRBC cytosol (Maier et al., 2008), although the presence of two predicted transmembrane domains suggests it may also associate with membranes.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Dietz et al., 2014.

claim: PTP3 appears to localize to the iRBC cytosol.
source: SEMP1 and PF3D7_0702500 co-localize at the Maurer's clefts (Dietz et al., 2014), while PTP3 appears to localize to the iRBC cytosol (Maier et al., 2008), although the presence of two predicted transmembrane domains suggests it may also associate with membranes.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Maier et al., 2008.

claim: The presence of two predicted transmembrane domains in PTP3 suggests it may also associate with membranes.
source: SEMP1 and PF3D7_0702500 co-localize at the Maurer's clefts (Dietz et al., 2014), while PTP3 appears to localize to the iRBC cytosol (Maier et al., 2008), although the presence of two predicted transmembrane domains suggests it may also associate with membranes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the presence of transmembrane domains.

claim: One site (position 2694) on Var2CSA PfEMP1 exhibited significantly increased biotinylation upon FIKK4.1 deletion.
source: Of note, one site (position 2694) on Var2CSA PfEMP1 itself exhibited significantly increased biotinylation upon FIKK4.1 deletion, suggesting that it becomes more exposed.
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data.

claim: Position 2694 of Var2CSA PfEMP1 becomes more exposed upon FIKK4.1 deletion.
source: Of note, one site (position 2694) on Var2CSA PfEMP1 itself exhibited significantly increased biotinylation upon FIKK4.1 deletion, suggesting that it becomes more exposed.
evidence: This is an inference based on the increased biotinylation.

claim: Other nearby biotinylation sites on Var2CSA do not change upon FIKK4.1 deletion.
source: Other nearby biotinylation sites on Var2CSA do not change; the alterations leading to the defect in surface presentation may therefore be very subtle.
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data.

claim: The alterations leading to the defect in surface presentation of Var2CSA may be very subtle.
source: Other nearby biotinylation sites on Var2CSA do not change; the alterations leading to the defect in surface presentation may therefore be very subtle.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the limited changes observed.

claim: FIKK4.1 activity leads to altered protein dynamics in the local environment of the cytoadhesion complex, including some previously identified PfEMP1 trafficking proteins.
source: Collectively these results indicate that FIKK4.1 activity leads to altered protein dynamics in the local environment of the cytoadhesion complex, including some previously identified PfEMP1 trafficking proteins.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: Other exported FIKK kinases localize to the periphery of the RBC or the Maurer's clefts.
source: Since other exported FIKK kinases localize to the periphery of the RBC or the Maurer's clefts (Davies et al., 2020; Nunes et al., 2010), we wanted to test whether any of the FIKK kinases in addition to FIKK4.1 play a role in the surface translocation of PfEMP1.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Davies et al., 2020 and Nunes et al., 2010.

claim: Only FIKK4.1 showed a significant reduction in anti-Var2CSA antibody binding under the conditions tested.
source: Only FIKK4.1 showed a significant reduction in anti-Var2CSA antibody binding under the conditions tested here (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The reduction in antibody binding upon FIKK4.1 deletion is unlikely caused by misfolding of Var2CSA PfEMP1.
source: This reduction in antibody binding is unlikely caused by misfolding of Var2CSA PfEMP1 as a reduced signal is observed upon FIKK4.1 deletion using four different antibodies raised against various domains of the protein (antibodies kindly gifted by Lars Hviid, University of Copenhagen) (Barfod et al., 2007; Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5B and a citation to Barfod et al., 2007.

claim: The defect in Var2CSA presentation upon FIKK4.1 deletion arises from reduced PfEMP1 exposure on the iRBC surface rather than changes in the conformation of the extracellular region.
source: This suggests that the defect arises from reduced PfEMP1 exposure on the iRBC surface rather than changes in the conformation of the extracellular region, as this would be less likely to affect all domains equally.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that multiple antibodies show reduced binding.

claim: Treatment of FIKK4.1 cKO parasites selected for CD36 binding with rapamycin results in a 51.5 ± 13% reduction in cytoadhesion under flow to CHO cells expressing CD36.
source: Treatment of these FIKK4.1 cKO parasites with rapamycin results in a 51.5 ± 13% reduction in cytoadhesion under flow to CHO cells expressing CD36 (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by adhesion assay data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: FIKK4.1 deletion results in a 54% reduction in binding of Var2CSA-expressing parasites to CSA-expressing HBEC-5i cells.
source: This is similar to the 54% reduction in binding of Var2CSA-expressing parasites to CSA-expressing HBEC-5i cells (Figure 5D), suggesting that FIKK4.1 likely has a general role in modulating PfEMP1 surface translocation, and our previous observations were not limited to Var2CSA PfEMP1.
evidence: This claim is supported by adhesion assay data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: FIKK4.1 likely has a general role in modulating PfEMP1 surface translocation.
source: This is similar to the 54% reduction in binding of Var2CSA-expressing parasites to CSA-expressing HBEC-5i cells (Figure 5D), suggesting that FIKK4.1 likely has a general role in modulating PfEMP1 surface translocation, and our previous observations were not limited to Var2CSA PfEMP1.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that multiple PfEMP1 variants are affected.

claim: A difference in binding between the FIKK4.1 KO and wildtype parasites is apparent at a slow flow rate of 4.5 mL/hr.
source: A difference in binding between the FIKK4.1 KO and wildtype parasites is already apparent at this point, suggesting that some cells lose their ability to bind CSA entirely (Figure 5F).
evidence: This claim is supported by adhesion assay data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Some FIKK4.1 KO cells lose their ability to bind CSA entirely.
source: A difference in binding between the FIKK4.1 KO and wildtype parasites is already apparent at this point, suggesting that some cells lose their ability to bind CSA entirely (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is an inference based on the adhesion assay data.

claim: By gradually increasing the flow rate to 150 mL/hr, a much stronger reduction in binding was observed in the FIKK4.1 KO line, indicating that the avidity of binding is also affected.
source: By gradually increasing the flow rate to 150 mL/hr, a much stronger reduction in binding was observed in the FIKK4.1 KO line, indicating that the avidity of binding is also affected.
evidence: This claim is supported by adhesion assay data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: One RIFIN was differentially phosphorylated upon FIKK4.1 deletion.
source: We previously found that one RIFIN was differentially phosphorylated upon FIKK4.1 deletion, suggesting that the kinase may also be important for its trafficking (Davies et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Davies et al., 2020.

claim: No difference in RIFIN surface translocation was observed upon FIKK4.1 deletion.
source: No difference was observed upon FIKK4.1 deletion (Figure 5G and H), suggesting that FIKK4.1 is restricted to the trafficking of PfEMP1, indicating that there are independent mechanisms for the surface translocation of RIFINs and potentially other surface proteins.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5G and H.

claim: FIKK4.1 is restricted to the trafficking of PfEMP1.
source: No difference was observed upon FIKK4.1 deletion (Figure 5G and H), suggesting that FIKK4.1 is restricted to the trafficking of PfEMP1, indicating that there are independent mechanisms for the surface translocation of RIFINs and potentially other surface proteins.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that RIFINs are not affected by FIKK4.1 deletion.

claim: There are independent mechanisms for the surface translocation of RIFINs and PfEMP1.
source: No difference was observed upon FIKK4.1 deletion (Figure 5G and H), suggesting that FIKK4.1 is restricted to the trafficking of PfEMP1, indicating that there are independent mechanisms for the surface translocation of RIFINs and potentially other surface proteins.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential effects of FIKK4.1 deletion on PfEMP1 and RIFINs.

claim: PerTurboID can complement other global methods probing protein accessibility such as limited proteolysis with mass spectrometry (LiP-MS) or thermal protein profiling.
source: PerTurboID can therefore complement other global methods probing protein accessibility such as limited proteolysis with mass spectrometry (LiP-MS) (Cappelletti et al., 2021) or thermal protein profiling (Savitski et al., 2014), with the targeted approach potentially allowing for a finer dissection of a specific subcellular niche and overcoming difficulties in capturing low-abundance proteins in whole-cell preparations.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Cappelletti et al., 2021 and Savitski et al., 2014.

claim: PerTurboID has the potential to investigate many changes to the local protein environment, including measuring the effects of drug treatment and external stressors, as well as measuring temporal changes such as membrane protein trafficking across time.
source: While we apply this technique to cell perturbation by gene deletion, it has the potential to investigate many other changes to the local protein environment, including to measure the effects of drug treatment and external stressors, as well as in measuring temporal changes such as membrane protein trafficking across time.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential applications of PerTurboID.
